title: Consensus with Raft
goal: By the end you can explain how Raft turns lesson 3's single Paxos decision into a replicated log, trace an election, the replication and commit of a log entry and a leader crash using terms, votes, AppendEntries and the commit rule, say how a leader serves a linearizable read and why membership changes go one server at a time, and build the core of Raft in a deterministic simulator.

warmup.q: Lesson 3's Paxos chose one value once a majority of acceptors accepted it. Raft uses majorities the same way, for every entry of a log. Five servers run Raft. The leader appends a payment to its log and sends it to the four followers. Two of them reply that they stored it. When may the leader tell the client the payment is saved?
options: Now: the leader and two followers make three of five, a majority
Only after all four followers have stored it
As soon as the leader has written it to its own disk
After the next heartbeat confirms that every follower is alive
warmup.why: Raft commits an entry of the current term once a majority of servers store it, the leader included. Any later leader must win votes from a majority, which shares a server with these three, and that server only votes for a log that holds the payment. Waiting for all four would let one slow follower stall every write. The leader's own disk alone survives a crash but not the loss of that machine.

sections.h: Paxos decides one value, and a database needs a log of them
sections.body:
Lesson 3 decided one value with Paxos. A proposer sends prepare to a majority of acceptors, then accept, two round trips, and because any two majorities share an acceptor, a value once chosen stays chosen. It also showed what a database needs instead of one value: a log, numbered commands such as debit A-1001, credit M-2001, settle batch 17, that every replica applies in the same order. And it named the shortcut that gets there, Multi-Paxos, where a stable leader runs phase 1 once for every future slot and then pays one round trip per command.

What lesson 3 left open is everything around that shortcut. Who becomes leader, and when? How does a new leader find out which slots its predecessor left half-decided? How does a crashed server catch up, and how do servers join and leave? "Paxos Made Simple" sketches the gap-filling and leaves the rest to the implementer, so every team that built Multi-Paxos answered on its own, and Google's "Paxos Made Live" (2007) lists what it took for Chubby.

Raft, published by Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout in 2014, answers all of them, and it was designed to be easy to implement. It keeps Multi-Paxos's shape: one leader at a time, a majority for every decision, one round trip per write. It adds rules that make the rest mechanical. Time is cut into numbered terms with at most one leader each. Only the leader appends to the log, and entries flow one way, from the leader to the followers. A server can win an election only if its log already holds every committed entry, so a new leader never has holes to fill. In the paper's study, 33 of 43 students scored better on a Raft quiz than on a Paxos one.

The figure is Raft's picture, and the rest of the lesson builds on it. Every server keeps a log. One leader takes every write and copies its log to the others. An entry is committed once a majority stores it, and every server applies committed entries, in log order, to its own copy of the data, which Raft calls the state machine. Five servers survive two failures and three survive one: 2f + 1 servers survive f. The next three sections build the parts: choosing the leader, copying the log, and keeping a committed entry safe when the leader dies. The last one covers what production systems add on top: safe reads, changing the members, and Kafka's version of Raft.

sections.h: Terms and votes elect one leader at a time
sections.body:
Every Raft server is a follower, a candidate or a leader. All of them start as followers. A follower that hears nothing from a leader for its **election timeout** assumes the leader is gone and starts an election. A leader prevents that by sending AppendEntries messages well inside the timeout (every 50 ms in the lab's simulator), empty ones, called heartbeats, when there is nothing to copy.

Raft numbers its periods of leadership with **terms**: 1, 2, 3 and so on, each beginning with an election. Every message carries the sender's term. A server that sees a higher term than its own adopts it and becomes a follower, and a request with a lower term is refused. So an old leader that was cut off learns it has been replaced from the first reply it gets, and nobody acts on its stale messages.

An election runs like this. The follower adds one to its term, becomes a candidate, votes for itself and sends RequestVote to every other server. A server grants at most one vote per term, to the first candidate that asks (plus one condition that a later section adds), and writes the vote to disk before it answers, so a crash and restart can't make it vote twice. A candidate with votes from a majority becomes leader and sends heartbeats at once, which resets everyone else's timer. Two leaders in one term would need two majorities that share no server, and five servers can't form those.

What if two followers time out together? Both become candidates in the same term, each votes for itself, and the votes split: two and two, say, with the fifth vote lost or late. Nobody has a majority, both time out again and retry in a higher term. With equal timeouts this could repeat forever. Raft draws each timeout at random, from 150 to 300 ms in the paper, so one server usually times out well before the others and collects its votes before anyone else wakes up. The paper measured the difference on five servers. With no randomness, electing a leader took more than 10 seconds because of repeated split votes. With only 5 ms of randomness the median time without a leader fell to 287 ms, and with 50 ms of randomness the worst of 1,000 trials took 513 ms. Shorter timeouts elect faster: with 12 to 24 ms, a leader was in place after 35 ms on average (152 ms at worst).

They can't shrink forever. Raft needs `broadcastTime ≪ electionTimeout ≪ MTBF`. The broadcast time is one round of messages to every server and back, including the write to disk each server makes before it answers: 0.5 to 20 ms in the paper's estimate. It has to fit into the timeout many times over, or followers start elections against a healthy leader whose heartbeat was merely slow. The timeout in turn has to be tiny next to the months between server failures (MTBF), because after a crash the cluster has no leader for about one timeout. That puts the timeout between 10 and 500 ms. etcd ships with a 100 ms heartbeat and a 1,000 ms election timeout, and its docs suggest a timeout of at least ten network round trips.

The lab's simulator makes this visible: five servers on a simulated network where each message takes 1 to 10 ms, and a seed that fixes every random choice. In the Try it, n4 times out first at 186 ms and wins at 192 ms. With every timeout fixed at 150 ms and every message at 5 ms, the five servers time out together, vote for themselves, refuse each other, and still have no leader after 10,000 ms and 330 elections.

sections.h: AppendEntries copies the log, and one check keeps the copies equal
sections.body:
A client sends the leader a command, a payment. The leader appends it to its log as an **entry**: the command plus the leader's current term, at the next index. Then it sends AppendEntries to each follower with the new entries and two numbers about the entry just before them, its index (`prevLogIndex`) and its term (`prevLogTerm`). A follower accepts only if its own log holds an entry at that index with that term. If it does, it deletes any entries of its own from that point on that conflict with the new ones, and appends what it doesn't have.

That one check keeps every log consistent. An empty log matches the start of any log, and each accepted AppendEntries extends a matching prefix with matching entries. So by induction, if two logs hold an entry with the same index and term, they hold the same command there and the same entries before it. Raft calls this the **Log Matching Property**: comparing one (index, term) pair tells you the whole history up to it is the same.

When the check fails, the follower's log differs somewhere earlier: it missed entries while it was down, or it holds entries from an old leader that were never committed. The leader keeps a `nextIndex` for each follower, the next entry to send it. On a refusal it moves `nextIndex` back by one and tries again, earlier, until the two logs agree; the follower then drops its conflicting tail and takes the leader's entries. The leader never deletes anything from its own log. Lost messages need no special handling: the next heartbeat resends everything from `nextIndex`.

The leader also keeps a `matchIndex` per follower: how far that follower's log is known to match. Once a majority has an entry, counting the leader itself, the entry is committed. The leader applies it to its state machine and answers the client, and the followers learn the new commit index from the `leaderCommit` field of the next AppendEntries and apply it too. In the normal case a write costs one round trip to the fastest half of the followers, so one slow follower slows nobody down. Every server must force entries to disk before it says it has them, so the fsync from the Storage engines track sits on this path too.

In the Try it, 16 of 152 messages are lost and every payment still commits, some a few dozen milliseconds later than the others. Two followers crash and the leader keeps committing with the three servers left. When a third follower crashes, the leader can't reach a majority: the next payment waits, uncommitted, until a crashed follower comes back and catches up.

sections.h: A new leader must already have every committed entry
sections.body:
Leaders crash, and the server that takes over may have missed entries. If a server missing a committed entry could become leader, it would force its log onto the others and delete an entry a client was told is saved. Raft stops this in the vote. RequestVote carries the index and term of the candidate's last log entry, and a voter refuses a candidate whose log is less up to date than its own: the log whose last entry has the higher term is more up to date, and with equal last terms the longer log is. A committed entry is on a majority, a winner needs votes from a majority, the two majorities share at least one server, and that server only votes for a candidate whose log holds everything its own does. So every new leader already has every committed entry.

One trap is left, shown in Figure 8 of the paper. A new leader finds an entry from an earlier term in its log, stored on a majority. Is it committed? Not necessarily: a server whose last entry has a newer term could still win an election and overwrite it. So a Raft leader commits only entries of its own term by counting copies, and older entries become committed when an entry of the current term after them does. That is why the lab's leaders append a no-op entry when they win: it gives them something of their own term to commit at once, and everything before it commits with it.

The stepper follows one payment through a leader crash and one election that a server loses because its log is behind. Not every entry survives a crash. An entry the old leader couldn't copy to a majority was never committed, so its client never got an answer, and a new leader may replace it. The client times out and retries. The paper's advice is to give every command a unique serial number, so the state machine can spot a retry and not apply it twice: an idempotency key, in the words of a payments team. The Try it shows the hardest case: an old leader cut off by the network keeps accepting a write it can never commit, until it hears a higher term and throws that entry away.

This is the machinery inside etcd, which stores the state of a Kubernetes cluster, inside CockroachDB, which runs one Raft group per range of keys, and inside Kafka's controllers, in a dialect the next section describes. PostgreSQL doesn't use Raft. Its failover managers, such as Patroni, keep the record of which server is primary in a consensus store such as etcd, so the agreement still comes from a protocol like this one.

With its own vote S3 has 4 of 5, more than the 3 it needs: **S3 leads term 1**. It appends a no-op entry of its own term (this section says why) and starts sending AppendEntries every 50 ms.

sections.h: Reads, membership changes and Kafka's pull-based dialect
sections.body:
Three things sit outside the core algorithm, and each has caught out real systems.

The first is reads. A leader holds every committed entry, so it is tempting to answer reads from its own state machine without asking anyone. But a leader can be deposed without knowing it: in the last Try it, the cut-off n2 still believed it led term 1 while n1 committed pay-3. A read served by n2 would miss pay-3 after other clients had seen it, which breaks lesson 2's rule for linearizability. Sending every read through the log works, but then a read costs as much as a write. The paper gives two cheaper ways. With **ReadIndex**, the leader notes its commit index, confirms it still leads with one round of heartbeats to a majority, waits until it has applied that index, and answers: one round trip and no disk write. A new leader must commit its no-op first, or it doesn't know its own commit index. With a **lease**, the leader relies on the fact that followers won't start an election until a timeout after they last heard from it, and answers locally until then: no round trip at all, but it is only safe if clocks advance at nearly the same rate and the leader isn't paused, the two hazards of the Faults, time and truth track's lessons on clocks and process pauses. etcd serves its default linearizable reads with ReadIndex, and the Raft library in etcd 3.7 hardened that path against stale reads.

The second is changing the members. Servers switch to a new configuration at different moments, so for a while some count majorities of the old set and some of the new. Going from three servers straight to five lets two old servers and three new ones elect two leaders in one term. The paper's answer is joint consensus, a transition entry during which every decision needs a majority of both sets. Ongaro's thesis later offered a simpler rule: change one server at a time, since any majority of n servers overlaps any majority of n + 1 or n - 1. In July 2015 he announced on the raft-dev list that this alone is unsafe. From four servers, a term-1 leader added S5 and reached only S5 before going offline; a term-2 leader then removed S1 and committed that on S2 and S3; S1 won term 3 with votes from S1, S4 and S5 and overwrote the committed entry. Two CMU students found it while formalizing the protocol. The fix is one rule: a leader may not start a membership change until it has committed an entry of its own term, its no-op.

The third is Kafka. Since Kafka 4.0 (March 2025) the cluster's metadata, topics, partitions and which broker leads what, lives in a Raft log called `__cluster_metadata`, run by three or five controllers. KRaft is Raft turned around: followers pull. Each follower sends Fetch with its log end offset and the epoch of its last entry. The leader answers with new records, or with a `DivergingEpoch` that tells the follower where its log parted from the leader's and where to truncate. A fetch doubles as the heartbeat, so a voter that gets no successful fetch within its timeout starts an election. An epoch is a term and the high watermark is the commit index, and a new leader writes a leader-change record and moves the high watermark only once an entry of its own epoch is on a majority, which is Figure 8's rule. Pulling lets every broker follow the metadata log as an observer that never votes, the way Kafka followers already copy partitions.

KIP-595: A Raft protocol for the metadata quorum

analogy: A Raft cluster works like a board that keeps signed minutes. Each period has one chair, elected by a majority of the members; the chair writes every decision into the minutes and sends each member a copy to sign; a decision counts once a majority has signed it. A member asked to elect a new chair refuses anyone whose copy of the minutes is older than its own, so a new chair always holds every signed decision. The analogy breaks at the meeting room. Board members can see who is present, while a Raft server can't tell a dead colleague from a slow network, which is why every rule runs on timeouts and term numbers instead of on knowing who is alive.
in_your_world: Your Kafka 4 clusters run Raft already: the KRaft controllers keep the cluster's metadata in a Raft log, which is why you run three or five of them, and why a controller quorum that loses two of three can't create a topic. Kubernetes keeps its state in etcd, another Raft group. In the payments database the question is the primary's replicas. PostgreSQL's default asynchronous replication can lose the last committed transactions on failover, so a payments primary usually waits for at least one synchronous standby (`synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (...)'`), and a failover manager such as Patroni decides who is primary through a consensus store such as etcd. Oracle Data Guard makes the same trade with its protection modes: synchronous transport so nothing committed is lost, or asynchronous for speed. Either way, a write that was accepted but not committed can disappear in a failover, and the client sees a timeout, not an error. That is the strongest argument for idempotency keys on every payment request: the retry after a failover must not charge the card twice.
mistake: The common mistake is sizing a consensus cluster by intuition: running two or four nodes for "more redundancy", or three nodes across two data centres. Four Raft servers need three for a majority, so they survive one failure, exactly like three servers, while every write waits for one more copy. Three servers split two and one across two sites lose their majority whenever the site with two goes down. People make it because more machines feel safer, and nothing goes wrong until the day a node or a site fails. The fix is odd sizes, three or five, spread over three failure domains (three availability zones), so that losing any one domain leaves a majority. Five servers survive two failures; going beyond five mostly adds write latency.

a.src:
synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 2 (s1, s2, s3)'

b.label: Raft
b.title: five servers
b.src:

the leader is elected by majority vote
failover: a follower times out, wins term n+1
who is leader: part of the protocol (terms)
votes go only to up-to-date logs

compare.note: Both wait for a majority of copies before a commit counts, so neither loses an acknowledged write when one server dies. The difference is who decides which server is in charge. PostgreSQL leaves it to an operator or an external tool, which itself needs a consensus store to avoid two primaries. Raft decides it inside the protocol, and its election rule guarantees that the new leader already holds every committed entry.

steps: Read `Messages.kt`, then the provided half of `RaftNode.kt` below the "provided" line: `receive` (it moves to a higher term for you), `tick`, `startElection` and `becomeLeader`. `Cluster.kt` runs five nodes on a simulated network and checks the safety rules every millisecond. Run the tests once: all 14 fail.
Write `handleRequestVote`. The first two tests pass.

Write `handleAppendEntries`: the term check, the log matching check, cutting a conflicting tail, appending, and the follower's commit index. Four more pass: the older-term test and the three follower tests.
Write `handleAppendReply` and `advanceCommitIndex`. The three leader tests pass, including the Figure 8 test.

Run all 14. The five cluster tests need all four handlers: they elect leaders, lose 10% to 15% of messages, crash and restart servers and cut one off the network. If one fails, print `c.events` in the test to read the timeline.
hints: In `handleAppendEntries`, check `req.prevLogIndex > lastLogIndex` before you call `termAt(req.prevLogIndex)`, or you read past the end of the log.
Never delete entries that match. A late, shorter copy of an old AppendEntries arrives after a newer one; it must leave the newer entries in place. Only a term mismatch at the same index cuts the log.
The follower's commit index is `maxOf(commitIndex, minOf(req.leaderCommit, req.prevLogIndex + req.entries.size))`: it follows the leader, never passes what this request proved, and never goes back.

In `advanceCommitIndex`, walk from `lastLogIndex` down to `commitIndex + 1` and stop at the first entry that is not from `currentTerm`. Count `matchIndex[i] >= n` over all servers; the leader's own entry is `matchIndex[id]`, which `propose` keeps up to date.

Write `handleAppendEntries(req)` for a follower whose `receive` has already adopted any higher term: the term check, the log matching check on `prevLogIndex`/`prevLogTerm`, the loop that keeps matching entries and cuts at the first conflict, and the commit index. recap: Paxos decides one value; Multi-Paxos runs one decision per log slot with a stable leader; Raft fills in the rest with terms, a one-way log and an election rule.

A follower that hears no leader for a random timeout (150 to 300 ms in the paper; 1,000 ms by default in etcd) starts an election in a new term; each server votes once per term. Without randomness, split votes kept elections going for over 10 seconds.
AppendEntries carries `prevLogIndex` and `prevLogTerm`; a follower accepts only if its log has that entry, which keeps logs identical up to any matching (index, term).

An entry is committed once a majority stores it, and a leader counts copies only for entries of its own term (Figure 8). Voters refuse candidates with less up-to-date logs, so every new leader holds every committed entry.

A leader's read is linearizable only after ReadIndex (a heartbeat round to a majority) or within a clock-based lease. Membership changes go one server at a time, and only after the new leader commits its no-op, or through joint consensus.

Raft runs inside etcd, CockroachDB and Kafka's KRaft controllers, which pull the log instead of having it pushed. PostgreSQL replicates its WAL instead and relies on tools such as Patroni, often backed by etcd, to pick a primary.

quiz.q: A Raft leader answers reads from its own state machine without contacting anyone. A partition cuts it off, the other four servers elect a new leader, and the new leader commits a refund that a second client reads. A third client now reads from the old leader. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: a Raft leader holds every committed entry, so its reads are always current
The read can miss the refund that another client already saw, which breaks linearizability; ReadIndex would have made the old leader check with a majority first and find out it was deposed
The read blocks until the partition heals
The old leader can't answer at all, because it sees the new leader's higher term
quiz.why: Leader Completeness says a leader holds every entry committed before its term began, not entries committed after it was deposed. The old leader hasn't heard the higher term yet, so it doesn't know it lost anything, and it answers with data older than what the second client saw: exactly the history lesson 2 calls non-linearizable. ReadIndex needs a heartbeat round with a majority before answering, which a cut-off leader can't complete.

quiz.q: A candidate's log ends with index 8, term 2. A voter's log ends with index 5, term 3. Neither has voted in the current term. Does the voter grant its vote?
options: Yes: the candidate's log is longer
Yes: the voter hasn't voted in this term
No: the voter's last entry has a higher term, so its log is more up to date
Only if the candidate's term is higher than 3
quiz.why: Raft compares the terms of the last entries first, and only on a tie compares lengths. The voter's term-3 entry may be committed; a leader whose log ends in term 2 doesn't have it and could overwrite it. A long log of old-term entries is worth less than one entry from a newer term.

quiz.q: The leader of term 4 finds an entry from term 2 at index 6 of its log. Three of five servers store it. May the leader mark index 6 committed now?
options: Yes: it is on a majority
No: it must first get an entry from term 4 onto a majority; index 6 is committed along with it
No: entries from old terms are always deleted by a new leader
Only if all five servers store it
quiz.why: This is Figure 8 of the Raft paper: an old-term entry on a majority can still be overwritten, because a server with a newer last term could win an election. So a leader commits only current-term entries by counting copies; once one is on a majority, everything before it is committed too. New leaders keep old entries, they don't delete them.

quiz.q: A network partition cuts the leader off from the other four servers. For ten seconds a client keeps sending it payments, and the leader appends each one to its log. What happens to those payments?
options: They are committed when the partition heals, because the leader logged them first
They are never committed: the leader can't reach a majority, its clients get no confirmation, and the new leader's log replaces them
They are committed at once, because a leader commits its own entries
Raft rejects them, because a partitioned leader knows it has lost its majority
quiz.why: Without a majority of copies nothing commits, so the clients never get an OK and time out. Meanwhile the other four elect a leader in a higher term. When the partition heals, the old leader sees the higher term, becomes a follower, and its uncommitted entries conflict with the new leader's log and are dropped. It doesn't know it is cut off; it only sees no replies, which is why the client must retry with an idempotency key.

quiz.q: From the Storage engines track's lesson on write-ahead logging: a follower replies success to AppendEntries before forcing the new entries to disk, then loses power. Why does that break Raft?
options: It doesn't: the leader still has the entry
The leader counted that follower toward the majority, so a committed entry may now be on fewer than a majority, and a leader elected without it could overwrite it
The follower will vote twice in the same term
AppendEntries will fail forever on that follower
quiz.why: Commit means "on a majority of disks". If one of the three copies vanishes in the power loss, only two servers hold the entry; a new leader can win with votes from servers that lack it and replace it, and a client was already told it is saved. That is the write-ahead log's commit rule again: say it is stored only after the log is forced. Its vote (`votedFor`) must be on disk for the same reason.

flashcards.front: How does a Raft leader serve a linearizable read without writing to the log (ReadIndex)?
flashcards.back: It notes its commit index, confirms it still leads with a heartbeat round to a majority, waits until it has applied that index, then answers. One round trip, no disk write.

flashcards.front: What went wrong with Raft's one-server-at-a-time membership changes (2015)?
flashcards.back: Two changes started from the same four-server config by different leaders gave configs whose majorities don't overlap. Fix: a leader commits an entry of its own term before any change.

flashcards.front: Why are election timeouts random, and how much does it matter?
flashcards.back: So one follower usually times out first and wins before the others start. In the paper, no randomness meant over 10 s of split votes; 5 ms of randomness gave a 287 ms median.

flashcards.front: What does a follower check before accepting AppendEntries?
flashcards.back: That its log holds an entry at `prevLogIndex` with term `prevLogTerm`. Otherwise it refuses and the leader steps `nextIndex` back.

flashcards.front: When does a Raft leader commit an entry?
flashcards.back: When a majority stores it and it is from the leader's current term. Earlier entries commit along with it.

flashcards.front: Which candidates does a server refuse to vote for?
flashcards.back: Those whose log is less up to date: an older last term, or the same last term and a shorter log. And any second candidate in a term it already voted in.

flashcards.front: What happens to an entry the old leader never got onto a majority?
flashcards.back: It was never committed and may be replaced by the new leader's log; the client got no OK and must retry, ideally with an idempotency key.

terms.plain: A linearizable read: the leader confirms with a majority that it still leads, then answers once it has applied its commit index.
Servers that can crash and lose messages agreeing on one value or one order of log entries.
More than half of the servers: 3 of 5. Any two majorities share a server.
Raft's numbered leadership period; at most one leader per term.
How long a follower waits without hearing a leader before it starts an election; random, about 150 to 300 ms.
The leader's message that copies log entries to a follower, or is an empty heartbeat.
If two logs have an entry with the same index and term, they are identical up to that entry.
An entry stored on a majority; it will never be lost and every server applies it in order.

explain_back.prompt: The leader of a five-server Raft cluster crashes right after it committed a payment that only two followers had stored. Explain why the payment can't be lost, using the vote rule.
explain_back.answer: The payment is committed, so it is on three servers: the old leader and two followers. To become the new leader, a candidate needs votes from three of the five servers. Any group of three must include at least one of the two followers that hold the payment, since the old leader is down and only two other servers lack it. A voter refuses any candidate whose log is less up to date than its own, comparing the term of the last entry first and the length second. A follower holding the payment therefore votes only for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own, which means a log that also holds the payment. So whoever wins already has it, and since a leader never deletes its own entries, it copies the payment to the others instead of overwriting it.

deeper.body:
**Log compaction.** A log can't grow forever. Each server snapshots its state machine, writes the snapshot to disk and discards the log up to that point (section 7 of the paper). A follower that falls too far behind gets the leader's snapshot instead of the entries, through a third message type, InstallSnapshot.

**PreVote and CheckQuorum.** A server cut off by a flaky link keeps timing out, raising its term, and on reconnecting forces a healthy leader to step down. PreVote makes a candidate first ask whether it could win before it raises its term; CheckQuorum makes a leader step down by itself when it stops hearing from a majority. Ongaro's thesis describes both, etcd-io/raft implements them, and lesson 5 shows a partial partition that left a three-node etcd cluster tied in elections.

**Many Raft groups.** One Raft group has one leader and one log, which limits its write rate. CockroachDB and TiKV split the key space into ranges and run one Raft group per range, thousands per cluster, so leaders spread across machines. Lesson 6 builds a distributed SQL database out of exactly that.

**Raft in the wild.** etcd, CockroachDB and TiKV run the etcd-io/raft library, and Consul runs HashiCorp's raft. The proofs assume that what a server acknowledged is on disk. Jepsen's 2025 analysis of NATS JetStream, which uses Raft but by default flushes to disk only every two minutes while acknowledging at once, lost 131,418 of 930,005 acknowledged messages in a simulated power failure: the last quiz question, at scale. DynamoDB's partitions use Multi-Paxos instead, as the Partitioning track's DynamoDB lesson shows.
